headlines.title: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CoreWeave, Salesforce, Rocket Lab, Kimberly-Clark & more
headlines.summary: Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading.
headlines.article_text: Stocks making the biggest moves midday: CRWV, CRM, RKLB, KMB Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Here are some of the companies making headlines in midday trading. Semiconductors — Chipmakers fell on Thursday, dragging the tech sector lower on the day. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH) is heading for its eighth losing day, down 2% in the session. Shares of Nvidia lost nearly 2%, while shares of Advanced Micro Devices and Marvell Technology fell more than 3%. Software makers — Software companies were a bright spot within the tech sector, with the iShares Expanded Tech-Software Sector ETF (IGV) adding about 1%. Shares of Salesforce gained almost 4%, while shares of Adobe rose more than 3%. Oracle 's stock climbed 2%. Consumer staples — Shares of consumer staples companies rose as investors fled the tech sector for relative safety. Campbell's stock added about 5%, and shares of General Mills and Conagra Brands gained more than 3% each. FMC Corp — Shares tanked 32% after the chemical manufacturing company slashed its guidance for the third quarter. The company now sees revenue in a range between $65 million and $125 million, sharply below the FactSet consensus estimate of $868.5 million. "Q3 demand was weaker than we expected, driven by challenging market conditions and elevated levels of higher-priced FMC products held in inventory by certain channel customers, which are limiting product movement and replenishment demand," said CEO Pierre Brondeau in a statement . Intuit — Shares added 6% after the company behind TurboTax and QuickBooks software announced that it will acquire Sequence , a revenue management platform. Kimberly-Clark — The maker of Huggies diapers saw its stock gain about 4% after it issued preliminary third-quarter results that topped Wall Street's estimates. The company earned $1.70 per share, excluding certain items, on revenue of $4.13 billion. That compares to the FactSet consensus call for $1.58 per share and $4.09 billion. Berkshire Hathaway — Shares ticked up 0.4% and headed for an 11th consecutive winning day. On Wednesday, Italian tech conglomerate Bending Spoons announced that Berkshire made a $330 million investment into the company. That's in addition to Berkshire's $600 million infusion into the company in July when Bending Spoons debuted on the Nasdaq. The RealReal — Shares rose 11% after the online marketplace for designer clothes announcrd that it has obtained a $150 million term loan as well as a $25 million senior secured revolving credit facility. The RealReal will use the proceeds to refinance its 2029 senior secured notes. Marsh & McLennan — The insurer saw shares jump 5% on the back of top- and bottom-line beats for the third quarter. Marsh reported adjusted earnings of $2.03 per share on revenue of $6.86 billion, compared with the FactSet consensus of $1.97 per share and $6.64 billion. The advance led the SPDR Insurance ETF (KIE) 1% higher on the day. CoreWeave — Shares of the cloud infrastructure technology company fell for a second day, losing 2% on Thursday as investors worry that CoreWeave, along with other technology companies, are borrowing too much for an artificial intelligence build-out. Artificial Intelligence infrastructure plays Nebius Group and Iren also slid 5% and nearly 8%, respectively. Shares of Dell Technologies lost 8%, and shares of data storage company Everpure fell 6%. Rocket Lab — The space company's stock dropped 11% after it delayed the launch of its Neutron rocket to 2027. SK Hynix — Shares of the South Korea-based company slid 2% as investors are concerned over funding the artificial intelligence build-out. The drop also follows a 7.6% drop in the South Korean Kospi index overnight. Penske Automotive — Shares popped 8% after the transportation company said it would be taken private by Motown Acquisition Corp., an entity owned by Penske Corp. and Mitsui, for $212 per share in cash. The deal represents a nearly 9% premium to Wednesday's closing price of $194.79 per share. The transaction is expected to close in the first quarter of 2027. Walmart — Shares of the retailer popped more than 2% after Deutsche Bank upgraded the stock to buy from hold, citing a positive outlook for 2027. The bank expects incremental margins to improve and noted current inflation levels could help the company attract consumers. Crocs — The footwear company's stock rose 6% after Barclays upgraded Crocs to overweight from equal weight. Analyst Adrienne Yih cited the company's progress on product innovation and category expansion and its international business growth as factors for the upgrade. — CNBC's Fred Imbert, Tom Rotunno and Nick Wells contributed reporting

TSMC chip capacity is ‘fierce’ battleground for AI customers, amid record quarter
headlines.summary: TSMC had a record quarter, but it can't make chips for everyone as Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom and AMD fight for capacity.
headlines.article_text: Nvidia, Apple, Broadcom in 'fierce' battle to make chips at TSMC Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points TSMC makes the vast majority of the world's most advanced chips, but soaring AI demand has sparked fierce competition for manufacturing capacity. Chip companies are cultivating relationships in Taiwan and making the case that they could become TSMC's next big customer. At the center of the competition is TSMC executive Kevin Zhang, who one customer describes as "the most popular person on the planet." In this article TSM Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 13:36 13:36 TSMC can't make chips for everyone, and competition is 'extremely fierce' Tech As Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.'s record quarter makes clear, demand from chipmakers shows no sign of slowing down. In fact, TSMC can't manufacture quickly enough. The artificial intelligence boom has created unending need for space on factory lines at the world's leading chip manufacturer, and it could put a chokehold on the entire industry's ability to scale. Last year, TSMC said it had the capacity to make more than 17 million 12-inch equivalent wafers. But customers want more. "The competition is extremely fierce," said Jordan Klein, an analyst at Mizuho Securities. "It's a game of who can get the most leverage and supply." TSMC makes the vast majority of the world's most advanced semiconductors, the graphics processors and central processors from Nvidia , AMD and Broadcom that are necessary for running AI workloads. Now a growing number of tech firms – Apple , Google , Amazon , Microsoft , Meta and OpenAI – also rely on TSMC to make custom in-house AI accelerators. TSMC North American CEO Sajiv Dalal told CNBC he gets at least 10 calls a day about wafer capacity. TSMC posted record profit for a sixth straight quarter on Thursday and expects fourth-quarter revenue to be 58% higher than a year earlier, driven by strong demand for its advanced chipmaking technologies. If compute demand continues to grow at the current rate over the next 12 to 18 months, Klein said capacity constraints at TSMC could threaten some of the industry's massive infrastructure investments and the "aggressive revenue growth targets" from the AI companies. U.S. hyperscalers are projecting well over $700 billion in capital expenditures this year, and analysts expect that figure to jump in 2027. AI ambitions are also threatened by a global shortage of memory chips. The logic chips that TSMC manufactures are more complex and expensive to produce. That means GPU and CPU leaders like Nvidia and AMD work out lengthy contracts and bespoke deals with TSMC behind closed doors years in advance. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and AMD CEO Lisa Su have both visited Taiwan multiple times this year. watch now VIDEO 3:33 03:33 This Nvidia challenger says its AI chip is 10x faster than a GPU Tech Sid Sheth, CEO of AI chip startup D-Matrix, has fostered a relationship with TSMC for more than 20 years, and his company relies on TSMC to manufacture its processors. For TSMC customers, many roads lead to Kevin Zhang, a senior vice president of the Taiwanese company and a central figure in determining which chipmakers get access to its coveted factory lines. He's "currently probably the most popular person on the planet," Sheth said in an interview. Sheth said that Jerry Qubain, D-Matrix's vice president of manufacturing, has been visiting TSMC since 1992 and goes to Taiwan three to four times a year. "This was even before Nvidia was founded," Sheth said. "That's a good example of a person we brought on board because of the relationships he has at TSMC." Qubain joined D-Matrix in 2024. TSMC declined to participate in this story. Betting on startups TSMC had 534 customers in 2025. While it doesn't name or rank them, its top 10 customers accounted for 78% of net revenue , with its top two bringing in 19% and 17%, respectively. That leaves startups competing for capacity against customers with far bigger orders. Sheth said TSMC is "selective," but has an incentive to back promising newcomers. "They were very supportive of Nvidia and Broadcom when they were very young companies, and now these are their biggest customers today," Sheth said. "They want to see a repeat of that." TSMC is hustling to bring much more capacity online, with new fabs in Taiwan, Japan and Arizona — it's making advanced chips in the U.S. for the first time. In July, TSMC announced it was adding $100 billion and "several more" fabs to the six planned in Arizona, bringing its total commitment to $265 billion. TSMC is also reportedly considering an entirely new fab location in Texas. watch now VIDEO 16:25 16:25 Inside TSMC's new chip fab where Apple will make chips in the U.S. Tech All of this will take years to come online. In the meantime, analysts say TSMC is adding tools like ASML's extreme ultraviolet lithography machines to existing factories to ramp up capacity. ASML smashed profit expectations in its earnings report Wednesday and said customers are interested in placing orders through 2030. TSMC isn't the only option. Capacity constraints create an opening for the other two leading advanced chip manufacturers, Samsung and Intel , to win customers. "People want a second source to be able to twist TSMC's arm and keep them honest on pricing," Dan Hutcheson, an analyst at TechInsights, told CNBC. That second source might be Intel, the only U.S.-based advanced logic manufacturer. Although its foundry business has been struggling with delays and setbacks for years, Hutcheson says all the big chipmakers are now testing there. Trade association SEMI expects 102 new chip fabs will come online globally by 2029, including 15 in the U.S. and 78 in Asia. China is the primary growth engine, expected to nearly triple capacity by 2030. In a race to catch up, American fab investments are projected to more than double by 2029. With an increasing Arizona presence and "extremely fierce" competition for wafer capacity, Klein says TSMC is "one of the best strategically positioned companies on the face of the planet." CoreWeave — a so-called neocloud company — has taken on more than $51 billion of debt and obligations to finance its AI infrastructure buildout. It last stood at 1,088 bps — a 33% week-over-week jump and 177% higher than a year ago. Coreweave's 5-year credit default swap spread Credit concerns are spreading into AI equities too. CoreWeave's stock was down again Thursday, adding to Wednesday's 15.5% nosedive . Other neocloud stocks were under similar pressure. Nebius was down 5% and Iren sank 8% in Thursday trading. Anxiety about AI overspending is also spreading. For instance, shares of Micron Technology and Advanced Micro Devices shed 4% and 6%, respectively, following a big sell-off in South Korean chip stocks. While AI debt worries have been rising steadily, investors have suddenly grown skittish about the underlying finances of companies borrowing heavily to buy chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power. Coreweave's credit default swaps are one place to see that stress. Credit default swaps are contracts where buyers pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. The spread widening in CoreWeave's CDS means investors view the debt as riskier. The market is "basically saying 'no mas' to AI debt without operating cash flow support," the Evercore ISI trading desk said. A spread level of 1,000 basis points or above is generally a sign of credit distress, said Gavan Nolan, executive director of fixed income pricing at S&P Global Market Intelligence. The backlog is over $100 billion, with around two-thirds of it with investment-grade counterparts including Microsoft , Meta , IBM and Caterpillar , Deutsche Bank said in a note Thursday. The firm reiterated its buy-rating on the stock Wednesday, calling the dislocation a buying opportunity. headlines.summary: A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks deepened Thursday.
headlines.article_text: AI stocks sell-off in global tech rout on AI funding worries Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Nvidia, AMD, Intel and Dell dropped on Thursday, as AI stocks across the globe continued to sell-off. Collectively, 20 of the most valuable global AI and semiconductor stocks have shed more than $1 trillion in value so far this week. The declines came as investors grew increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending In this article 9984.T-JP TSM ASM-NL NVDA SKHY ASML CRWV INTC NOK Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 4:36 04:36 Dave Mazza: Memory stocks are in transition Squawk on the Street Stocks tied to the artificial intelligence trade sank on Thursday, continuing a global sell-off. Collectively, 20 of the most valuable global AI and semiconductor stocks have shed more than $1 trillion in value so far this week, as interest rate hikes, AI financing and intensifying competition weighed on sentiment. Nvidia fell about 2% while AMD and Intel each lost about 4%. Dell Technologies sank 8%. Neoclouds also dropped, with CoreWeave sinking 3%, Nebius down 5% and IREN falling more than 8%. Micron was down about 5% earlier but turned positive around noon ET. Shares in the neoclouds pared some of the earlier losses after comments from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang seemed to settle fears in the AI trade. Huang told Bloomberg at an event in Stockholm, Sweden, that he didn't see a need for Nvidia to backstop CoreWeave and that, "Their cost of capital is actually decreasing." A sell-off in global technology hardware stocks also deepened across Asia and Europe on Thursday. South Korean chip giant SK Hynix plunged more than 10%, while rival Samsung Electronics fell 8.73%. Other South Korean chip-related stocks also came under pressure. LG Innotek sank 8.95%, Seoul Semiconductor shed 9.28% and Samsung SDI declined 6.26%. In Japan, technology investment giant SoftBank Group tumbled 7.9%. Semiconductor testing equipment maker Advantest plunged almost 14%, while chipmaking equipment supplier Tokyo Electron lost 6.45%. Renesas Electronics declined 8%. Taiwan's TSMC , the world's largest contract chipmaker, fell 1.81%. Over in Europe, Dutch semiconductor giant ASML was last down 5.2%, Infineon Technologies shed 8.2% and ASM International was down 8.6%. CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN stock chart. Why stocks are selling off The declines come as investors grow increasingly concerned that higher borrowing costs could weigh on the massive capital spending required to build out AI infrastructure, putting pressure on technology companies that have benefited from the AI investment boom. Concerns around global memory chip oversupply as early as 2029, as manufacturers ramp up production capacity to meet surging demand from artificial intelligence, also seem to be weighing down sentiment. China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , said over the weekend that it had made a breakthrough on a new architecture that could boost memory density by packing more data into a smaller space, signaling intensifying competition in the memory space. Elon Musk in an X post said China would be making "a LOT of RAM in 2028." Why this little known Chinese chipmaker has caused a global stock rout Chief executives of Broadcom and Intel, meanwhile, warned on Monday that financing could become a major headwind to the AI boom, with Broadcom's Hock Tan saying it could be bigger challenge to AI expansion than shortages of chips or electricity. The sell-off followed a bruising session on Wall Street Wednesday, where technology shares led broader market losses after hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation data fueled concerns that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates further. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite dropped 1.88% to close at 26,692.87, while the S&P 500 shed 1.11% to end at 7,718.94. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.09%. watch now VIDEO 6:59 06:59 Kospi on track for weakest close since April as global AI sell-off deepens Squawk Box Europe Dan Ives, tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, said the latest sell-off in AI-related stocks reflects growing concerns over the cost of financing massive infrastructure projects as U.S. Treasury yields climb above 5%, but added that underlying demand for AI computing power remains robust. "Higher yields raise the cost of financing these builds, and investors are right to focus on balance sheets and contract structure, but rates are a financing question, not a demand question," Ives said in a note. The latest pullback presents a buying opportunity, Ives said, adding that the AI infrastructure boom remained in its early stages despite mounting concerns over funding costs. "What would change our view is a demand signal, not a rate signal," he said, pointing to potential cuts in hyperscaler capital expenditure plans, canceled contracts or falling GPU rental prices as warning signs.
